cells.tense: The spark is here right now, and the pen is in your hand.
cells.act: think it through to its sharp point
cells.ask: Before you start the next thing, take ten quiet minutes and find the claim it rests on. Then begin.
cells.core:
Starting is easy for you — an idea strikes and the fire catches. What takes longer is standing under the weight once the first heat has burned off, and that is the shape of a long haul. Both are in you at once, and they don't fight each other.

Sit ten minutes with the next idea before any doing. Follow the thought down to the claim it actually rests on, one point, and only then move. Starting light and starting clear are different things, and clear is what a long haul can use. You strike the spark and stand under what it becomes. Name the hinge first, and the standing is aimed.
cells.sheetLine: You strike the spark and then carry what it becomes.
cells.verb: lighting a fire for a direction before knowing where it leads
cells.place: bearing weight in the body over a long haul

cells.tense: You are bracing already for a future that cannot be written in.
cells.act: ask the question you do not know the answer to
cells.ask: Set a plan aside for a day and ask a plain question about it you can't answer. Let the answer sit without deciding.
cells.core:
You are loading the next step onto your back before the ground is laid under it. Plans stack up in front of the moment, and you carry the whole pile to prove it can be done. Nobody asked you to hold it at once, only to take the step that is here.

A question weighs less than a plan. Put one aside for a day and ask a plain thing about it that you don't already know — of someone who knows a piece of it, or of the work itself. Let the answer sit without building on it. You don't have to be certain to keep going. Stand where you actually are, three moves back from where you were leaning, and the fire will carry what it needs to.

cells.tense: The starting fire went out, and you are still standing in its doorway.
cells.act: care for it with fresh hands and see what it needs
cells.ask: Take a plant or a page of work that's been sitting. Give it five minutes of looking, and notice what it needs from your hands.
cells.core:
A spark is behind you, and the doorway it opened is one you didn't step through. From outside it can look as if you have stopped starting. From inside it is quieter — the energy for a direction just isn't reaching your hands right now.

Don't push at that. Go to a small live thing instead — a plant on a sill, a page of work left mid-sentence, a square of something larger. Give it five minutes of looking, and let what it asks of your hands become the whole of the task. Care for something alive and it hands back some fuel, which is the thin part. Tend what's growing, and a foot goes inside the door.

cells.tense: The pen is already moving in your hand, and it is not being signed.
cells.act: hold the weight as a builder holds stone
cells.ask: Each week, add a line to a note: what you kept standing for others, and the hours it took. No one else has to see it.
cells.core:
You hold plenty steady without naming it — routines that keep a household upright, weight taken quietly off other people, the piece that doesn't fall apart because your hands are under it. Your version has you just getting on, and that reads as not much. What it actually is is strength that keeps its shape under pressure, the kind used on stone. A whole week doesn't tip, and this is the reason.

The building is already yours. Start a short note, one line a week: the thing you kept standing, and what it cost you in hours. Nothing else has to change. Seeing the tally turns unnamed bearing into work that was done on purpose. You keep something upright that would otherwise lean.
cells.sheetLine: The steadying is your work, and you haven't signed it.
